en: That here in Talas we shall
Raise Kyyaz as khan!”
When Kanchoro had spoken thus,
As though pierced in a tender swelling,
Külchoro sprang to his feet:
“You were Chubak’s handsome son,
Three years older than I;
We kicked and tussled like foals,
And suckled at one another’s mothers’ breasts.
Among all the friends and kinsmen
Whose ears have heard and eyes have seen,
When has this bloodthirsty lion
Ever been called a child?
You wander and rave in your speech,
Rehearsing words of treachery;
You praise the Jediger’s Kyyaz
As though he were a monster!
Kanchoro, may a curse strike you!
May the spirits of our forefathers—
Almambet and the eagle Chubak,
The lions Syrgak and Serek,
And gray wolf Manas’s warriors—judge us!
If I should flinch and speak crookedly,
Make my words double-tongued,
Make my speech dishonorable,
And blacken my own face—
If, like you, Kanchoro,
I should sit here committing treachery,
May God strike me down at once!
You have spoken too many treacherous words,
And ended by saying
You would raise Kyyaz as khan;
With those words you have ruined everything.
Do you think Talas is an easy land to take?
The Argyn and Kyrgyz of Talas
Who inhabit the Seven Valleys—
Are they inferior to the Jediger?
May your Kyyaz sink into the earth!
Is he more heroic than our Semetey?
My lion-hearted uncle, khan of the age—
Is he any less than your Kyyaz?!
Who would listen to these words of yours?
Let some dark night listen,
Let a deep-dug pit listen!
You kept praising him, blustering away;
Let the army of Chochko’s Jediger hear,
Let the pampered bird hear!
Let the barking dog hear—
Who else would listen?
You base-born Kanchoro,
You black devil of a warrior,
There is insolence in your words
And treachery in your eyes.
If you have the strength, you rabid cur,
You mean to bring me down;
You speak words that make one gnaw the reins,
Foretelling a time of true calamity,
And swear by the realm of spirits—
Has God struck you mad?
If I do not gird my waist firmly,
If I do not drive the Jediger of the Seven Valleys
Back to every corner of their lands,
If I do not spill their blood,
If I do not slaughter all their people,
Then may the spirit of noble Manas
Hunt me down and strike me!
If not, may Choro, who consorts with demons,
Strike you down!
Damn you, Kanchoro,
I have seen what these people do—
So this is what you intended.
You base-born, crooked slave,
So you meant to reach me at last!
You meant to forsake this gray wolf
Blessed by Kyzır,
And find some cunning way
To bring about my end.
You sent a letter to the Jediger,
Summoned Kyyaz to your side,
And meant to take him with you;
You meant to plunge my head
Into grievous hardship.
Your true champion Kyyaz,
With six swift horses
And a letter no bigger than a palm—
You meant to bring him here
And stir up a mighty tumult,
A great conflict.
I have seen many strange people—
So this was what you meant to do,
You accursed bastard!
By finding the chance,
You meant to bring about my end.
Making Kyyaz your holy protector,
You bastard swine,
You meant to abandon me.
From the first, there was deceit in your words,
And treachery shone in your eyes;
If you had the strength, you rabid cur,
You meant to bring me down.
There was crookedness in your speech,
And guile in your eyes;
Watching for your chance and plotting,
You rabid cur, you meant to harm me.
You shameless bastard,
You meant to bring down upon me
A black day, misery, and great strife;
You meant to seize
The bloodthirsty hero’s wives.
You meant to reveal yourself midway
And go over, you dog,
To Kyyaz, with whom we are at war.
You meant to bring conflict
Upon the hero.
Yesterday, on the plain of Jylgynduu,
Along the broad Talas,
When, wearing matching sable caps,
I strutted proudly,
And we played together, singing laments,
In the midst of our rejoicing,
When we split a whole otter skin
Lengthwise between you,
And you swaggered like kings
With it sewn onto your cuffs—
Have you forgotten the honor you planted in Keng-Kol,
You accursed wretch?
Have you forgotten the days when you strode so proudly?!
Drinking kumis and courting girls,
Have you forgotten that happiness?
Can the sole heir of a khan
Rightly commit such treachery?
Can there ever be another fool
With thoughts as black as yours?
Can the only son of a noble
Harbor such evil intent?
Can a true kinsman prosper
Who plots against his own khan?
Is there any man like you,
Who would bring distress upon his lord?
If you shoot at one who shared your mother’s breast,
Can you prosper in the end?
Can any man be like you?”
So Külchoro
Spoke these words as if alarmed,
And renowned Choro spoke of the outrage.
When he had finished speaking thus,
The gray wolf, son of Manas,
The lion upheld by holy powers,
The steadfast warrior,
The dear lion with the ringing voice,
Flew into a towering rage;
Wisdom came to him from the unseen,
And he took offense at the two traitors:
“I gathered thoroughbreds and tended horses—
A curse upon all that labor
Spent on steeds like Arbuurul!
I raised brave men and gathered lions,
Yet never gained the least benefit—
A curse upon those men,
Upon my kinsmen Abyke and Köbösh!
Yet may I ever be grateful
To the one who turned enemies into brothers.
When I took you two cherished lions in,
When I made you mine,
Slaughtered ninety beasts for your feast,
Gave you rhyming names,
Carved up haunches for you to eat,
And had you both suck
At Kanykei’s breasts,
We uttered every blessing
That you might become true brothers.
We swiftly invoked Baabedin,
And called upon Allah by name;
We said you would counsel a renowned hero,
And if the two traitors circled in flight,
They would be supporting wings behind my back—
Those two vaunted traitors!
In the marshlands of Jylgynduu and Talas,
I said I had found twin brothers,
And while we reveled in delight,
My dear mother Kanykei,
Her senses overcome, said:
‘When Külchoro suckled,
My whole body thrilled,
My tiny soul cried aloud,
All my ten joints and eighty bones
Softened completely and trembled;
From the right breast Külchoro suckled,
Pure white milk surged forth—
He is your brother,’ she said.
My mother also said:
‘From the left breast Kanchoro suckled,
And the bones of my joints cracked;
When that child drank at my breast,
Every layer of my ribs and chest
Was torn apart,
And from my left breast black blood
Flowed and poured away—
A sure sign that Choro’s
Enmity was revealed.
Listen to these words you have heard,
Heed me, my son:
May this child come to nothing—
Alas, he appears an enemy to my eyes.’
Those were my mother’s words.
As though your father Manas had sired him,
Your dear mother Kanykei
Carried him without rest for nine months,
As though she herself had borne him.
Had you heeded my words before,
Külchoro, who drank the right breast,
Would have been your inheritance,
A loyal follower of your good counsel;
But your Kanchoro, who drank the left breast,
Is in his heart your enemy—
He appears a foe to my eyes.
Take care, my child, and hear my words:
If you continue raising Kanchoro,
He will become your calamity.
His enmity is revealed,
For from my breast, my foal,
Black blood flows and pours;
At heart he appears an enemy.
If sent against a foe, he will not support you;
Let the wretch go his way—
At heart he will never be your ally.
He is an unripe cucumber and will never grow sharp;
The first omen has appeared:
He is a calamity and will never form a loyal people.
If he lives and grows,
He will mature into a warrior,
Become the equal of heroic sons,
And answer your words with defiance;
Claiming to be your brother, he will fire his gun
And become your enemy.
He will sow discord among your people;
When you confront a battling foe,
He will blacken your face with shame,
Make hollows of your open eyes,
And bring your death upon you.
If this Choro survives,
He will strip you of your honor.
His faith is alien,
And at heart he is your enemy.
Your radiant father had the habit
Of treating his ancestral foes like brothers,
Pitying them as kin,
And so he would die
At the hands of those closest to him.
Find a brother from another place
And make him your support, she said;
This child is not your brother—
Finish him off, she said.
But I would not heed my mother;
Thinking, ‘What can one lone son do?’
I did not keep him apart from my equals.
